Performance evaluation of peer-assisted MPEG-DASH streaming in multi-user mobile scenarios
abstract: The dramatic surge in multimedia consumption has exposed the structural vulnerabilities of traditional client–server distribution models, particularly during massive concurrent demand peaks. While hybrid architectures offer a potential solution, their real-world effectiveness is fundamentally governed by the degree of content demand overlap—a factor that has remained largely under-explored in experimental literature. This paper addresses this gap by proposing SwarmLayer, a novel hybrid peer-to-peer (P2P) assisted streaming architecture designed as a transparent middleware between the DASH player and the content delivery infrastructure. The proposed architecture leverages a combination of core web technologies, including WebRTC for low-latency peer connectivity, Service Workers for request interception, and Protocol Buffers for efficient data serialization. By operating at the browser’s network layer, SwarmLayer enables direct segment exchange among peers without necessitating modifications to the media player or application logic. Central to this work is the formalization of the Content Overlap Ratio (COR), a probabilistic framework introduced to quantify the potential for peer collaboration as the likelihood that two arbitrary players request segments from the same media presentation. This metric allows for a systematic characterization of the relationship between user demand patterns and systemic distribution efficiency. The performance of the proposed architecture is evaluated using a controlled multi-user testbed that emulates vehicular streaming scenarios through time-varying bandwidth profiles derived from real 5G mobility traces. Experimental results demonstrate that even moderate content overlap (COR = 0.14) yields a 57.4% reduction in CDN traffic, with offloading gains reaching 91.7% in high-demand scenarios. Beyond bandwidth optimization, the analysis of Quality of Experience (QoE) indicators reveals that the peer-assisted layer significantly enhances playback stability by increasing buffer robustness and mitigating bitrate oscillations under non-stationary network conditions.

title: Lowering the cost of realism: Scalable formal verification of autonomous cyber defense via dynamic formal model switching
An evaluation of zero-trust framework implementations for Industrial Internet of Things
abstract: Interactions between different types of systems from various environments are increasing continuously due to the nature of business and commercial requirements. All of these interactions require a level of trust granted to each system to enable essential operations and functions while appropriately controlling access to data. This is essential to ensuring that data is accessed only by authorised and trusted users. For these reasons, zero-trust frameworks have been in the spotlight in the past few years. Zero-Trust frameworks assume that users and systems have been compromised and treat them as untrusted entities that require multiple levels of authorisation and security attributes to be considered trusted. This research explores different methodological and systematic designs to implementing static and machine-learning zero-trust frameworks in IIoT critical environments. It adopts a systematic methodology to evaluate the impact and benefits of the proposed approaches on both cybersecurity and operational safety. The outputs of these frameworks would inform observers about the trustworthiness of systems in their environments. Moreover, the performance, complexity, operational impact, and, most importantly, the security uplift of these approaches have been evaluated and compared, providing a holistic view of their advantages and disadvantages to determine the most suitable framework for IIoT solutions. The results presented in this research show clear advantages of using machine learning over static-threshold schemes in maintaining an essential balance between security and operational safety.

PVFL-CPN: A privacy-preserving vertical federated learning method for computing power networks
abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, demand for computing power and training data has reached unprecedented levels. Vertical Federated Learning, a promising distributed training method, can effectively address data shortage problems within a single organization. In addition, the emergence of computing power networks (CPNs) provides an ideal platform to address both runtime resource limitations and distributed training issues, also in complex scenarios characterizing modern cyber–physical systems. However, native VFL is susceptible to label, gradient, and model inference attacks. Therefore, to address all of the above challenges, we propose PVFL-CPN, a privacy-preserving VFL method for computing power networks based on homomorphic encryption and secret sharing. This approach uses masking-based one-time pad encryption to secure the forward and backward propagation processes in VFL, as well as to protect communication between computing nodes in CPN. PVFL-CPN outperformed its VFL competitors in terms of accuracy, computational cost, and communication efficiency.

Resilient SFC deployment in MEC: A dual approach with optimized redundancy and VNF splitting
abstract: The synergy of Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV) provides a flexible platform for deploying Service Function Chains (SFCs). However, the software-based nature of Virtual Network Functions (VNFs) introduces significant challenges to service resilience, making them prone to failures that can disrupt latency-sensitive applications. This paper addresses the critical problem of deploying cost-effective, resilient SFCs by exploring two fundamental reliability paradigms: traditional standby redundancy and innovative VNF splitting. While standby redundancy offers a straightforward path to fault tolerance, it often leads to inefficient resource utilization due to idle backups. Conversely, VNF splitting, which decomposes a VNF into active, load-sharing diverse replicas, promises greater resource efficiency but introduces new complexities in latency and management overhead. To navigate these trade-offs, we formulate the deployment problem as a cost-minimization task under strict reliability and latency constraints. We propose a dual algorithmic framework to tackle this challenge. For the non-splittable scenario, we design MDCA, an approximation algorithm with a provable performance guarantee. For the splittable scenario, we introduce DMDCA, a sophisticated heuristic that intelligently determines the optimal degree of VNF diversity and backup configuration. Extensive simulations based on a real-world dataset validate our approach. The results show that MDCA significantly reduces deployment costs compared to baseline methods, and DMDCA further enhances cost-efficiency by strategically leveraging VNF splitting.

Scalable modular digital twins for next-generation wireless networks: A spatial fusion framework
abstract: As Next-Generation 6G networks and smart city infrastructures grow in scale and complexity, Digital Twin (DT) technology has become essential for real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and network optimization. However, current state-of-the-art implementations rely heavily on massive, monolithic digital twins to model large-scale environments. These systems face severe architectural bottlenecks, suffering from compromised fidelity due to overwhelming complexity, poor scalability leading to high computational latency, and limited interoperability. To overcome these limitations, we propose a scalable spatial fusion framework based on Modular Digital Twins. By spatially partitioning the physical environment into independent, self-intelligent modules, our architecture enables distributed generation of high-fidelity RF propagation states using deterministic 3D ray tracing. These localized semantic states are subsequently integrated via a central Fusion Engine utilizing a confidence-weighted cell-wise aggregation algorithm. Extensive evaluations in a hyper-realistic smart city environment demonstrate that the proposed fused modular architecture reduces computation time by approximately 70.4% compared to a monolithic massive DT. Furthermore, it achieves this superior scalability and processing speed while maintaining high fidelity, exhibiting a marginal absolute Signal-to-Interference-plus-Noise Ratio (SINR) error of only 4.47 dB.

abstract: Satellite communications paired with Internet of Things (IoT) devices are playing a vital role across many industries. However, one of the key challenges in IoT-driven satellite (IoT-Satellite) networks is the vulnerability of satellites to spoofing and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. A proposed solution for improving the security of these complex networks is the use of software-defined networks (SDN), but this does not fully address challenges such as preventing spoofing and DoS attacks or enhancing network observability. While various machine learning (ML) models show promise in network traffic classification and anomaly detection for IoT and SDNs, most research is limited to specific use cases, such as GPS technologies, with less focus on SDNs. Additionally, current research prioritises model performance over evaluation in the context of real-world use cases. This paper compares existing ML-based solutions and develops a framework for evaluating appropriate ML approaches for IoT-Satellite network environments. It focuses on network segmentation using SDNs, based on both generic and use-case specific criteria. The models examined include k-means, convolutional neural networks (CNN), long short-term memory (LSTM), hidden Markov models (HMM) and random forest (RF). The results show that the most suitable models for IoT and SDN-based networks are HMM and RF. The HMM model demonstrated the best performance in detecting spoofing and DoS attacks across both networks, with high scores in latency and cross-network performance, followed closely by the RF model, which scored high in accuracy and medium in latency. Based on these findings, we propose future research into hybrid models and their integration with emerging technologies, such as blockchain, to enhance security in SDNs and IoT-satellite networks.

SereBench: Adversarial robustness benchmarking for security and reliability event classification in networked railway cyber–physical systems
abstract: This paper presents SereBench , an open-source security and reliability benchmarking framework for testing the adversarial robustness and federated resilience of AI-based attack and anomaly classification in networked railway Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). In this work, SereBench is instantiated and evaluated through a pneumatic braking subsystem case study, where pressure dynamics provide a physically interpretable basis for controlled robustness evaluation. The framework provides a simulation-based environment emulating a railway CPS system, enabling controllable class semantics and verifiable ground truth. This environment supports controlled adversarial robustness benchmarking by progressively stressing the decision boundaries of Machine Learning (ML) models. To this end, SereBench includes a train simulator that produces telemetry, preserving explicit cause–effect relations among signals and operating modes, allowing perturbations to be interpreted as changes in system behavior rather than as arbitrary feature edits. Adversarial robustness benchmarking can be executed in multi-vehicle settings, allowing the study of federated resilience effects, i.e., how robustness-related behavior changes across vehicles under model aggregation. The experimental campaign considers multiple classifier architectures and federated aggregation strategies, targeting the classification of security and reliability events under controlled robustness evaluation conditions. Specifically, the study explores configurations combining federated learning, noise-augmented training, controlled Gaussian boundary stress, and HSJA-based hard-label black-box adversarial evaluation. The experimental campaign also includes a focused FL-flow sensitivity analysis in which controlled message loss and delivery delay are applied to uplink and downlink model exchanges. The obtained results show that SereBench can support adversarial robustness benchmarking of ML models under controlled, braking-oriented railway CPS conditions.

A Survey on the Security of 5G and Beyond Networks in the Post-Quantum Era
abstract: With the rapid advancement of quantum computing, existing cryptographic schemes in 4G LTE and 5G networks confront serious security threats. Traditional reliance on protocols like IPsec and Transport Layer Security leaves infrastructure vulnerable to future quantum attacks, particularly “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” attacks, where adversaries store current encrypted traffic for future decryption. To counter these threats, Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have become potential solutions. As future 6G networks aim to realize ultra-reliable and ubiquitous secure connectivity, it is essential to incorporate both PQC and QKD solutions to ensure long-term robustness. Therefore, the synergy of these security solutions and 5G draws the attention of researchers and practitioners worldwide. This study systematically reviews the literature in this specific field. We analyzed evidence from reviewed literature to address three research questions, resulting in a novel taxonomy to categorize publications in this area and a vision for a quantum-safe 6G network. Moreover, we discussed several open challenges in 5G, PQC, and QKD, along with future work.

title: Uni-RAT: A unified DECT-2020 NR and Wi-Fi architecture for 6G Multi-RAT networks
abstract: Future 6G networks aim to deliver seamless, secure, and low-latency connectivity across heterogeneous radio access technologies (RATs) such as 5G New Radio (NR), Wi-Fi, and DECT-2020 NR to support emerging applications including extended reality (XR) and the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). However, current Multi-RATs systems are operated and managed in isolation, which hinders users and devices from seamlessly leveraging heterogeneous connectivity in a unified and efficient manner. To address this fragmentation, 3GPP has introduced interworking functions such as the N3IWF for untrusted and the TNGF for trusted non-3GPP access, enabling IP-session continuity when users move across heterogeneous networks. Nevertheless, these mechanisms rely on mandatory IPsec, which requires each RAT to maintain a separate secure tunnel to the core network and prevents intra-cell device-to-device (D2D) communication, thereby introducing significant encryption latency, increasing data-plane load, and complicating network management. To overcome these limitations, we propose Uni-RAT, a unified Multi-RATs framework in which DECT-2020 NR operates as the Master-RAT, anchoring 3GPP control-plane security via 5G-AKA and NAS, while Wi-Fi functions as a Secondary-RAT for data-plane data delivery. Uni-RAT employs lightweight Layer-3 WireGuard tunnels to secure both D2D and multi-hop communication, significantly reducing the latency and computational overhead of IPsec-based interworking mechanisms used by N3IWF and TNGF. In addition, a customized SMS-over-NAS signaling mechanism is introduced to distribute WireGuard configuration and keying material, enabling unified authentication and efficient Multi-RATs security management. We implement a full prototype using Nordic nRF9161 DECT-2020 NR devices, Raspberry Pi Wi-Fi nodes, and a Cumucore 5G core, with security-critical functions protected inside Arm TrustZone. Experimental results indicate that Uni-RAT supports Multi-RATs communication with high throughput and low packet loss in intra-cell D2D scenarios, maintains bounded latency and jitter under relay-assisted and inter-cell configurations, and achieves stable UE registration latency below 100 ms with up to 100 concurrent devices under background traffic, demonstrating its practical feasibility and scalability and positioning Uni-RAT as an early architectural blueprint for 6G Multi-RATs networks.

title: Load balancing in fog networks: a resource efficient service placement and task scheduling approach based on popular service sequences
HAPS as a proactive congestion-relief resource: Online control for cellular network management
abstract: Localized traffic peaks in cellular networks create transient high-load conditions that cannot be efficiently addressed through permanent densification. A high-altitude platform station (HAPS) can provide a repositionable aerial capacity layer that is dynamically steered toward emerging congestion, making it a flexible operational resource for radio access network (RAN) capacity management. Effective integration within an operational RAN, however, requires two coupled decisions. Limited beam resources must be allocated to cells approaching critical load before the next traffic realization is observed, while the platform must be positioned to maximize the service delivered to the selected cells. This leads to a demand–supply problem in which the selection layer determines the critical excess traffic made available for aerial offloading, whereas platform positioning determines how much service can actually be delivered. We propose a closed-loop framework combining a context-conditioned hierarchical selection policy, which ranks base stations (BSs) by exploiting recurrent temporal structure in operator traffic without explicit load forecasting, with a Lyapunov-based positioning controller that maximizes aggregate throughput under a long-term incremental maneuver-energy budget. Evaluation using real operator traffic traces shows that a single HAPS removes up to 64% of network-wide critical excess traffic, while controlled mobility provides up to a 24% throughput gain over a stationary deployment. The results further show that congestion relief does not scale uniformly with the beam budget: selection accuracy drives performance at small budgets, whereas platform geometry becomes the limiting factor as the assisted set expands.

title: CRNN: End-to-end collision recovery for RFID signals using deep neural networks

Autoscaling of Internet of Things applications in serverless edge computing
abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) services are deployed in edge clouds, which are close to end-users’ devices, when service latency is an important constraint, as often occurs. However, latency control cannot be achieved with ample resource allocation as in core clouds, since in edge environments resources are limited and thus operational efficiency is essential. Serverless computing, an emerging service model for both edge and core clouds, may help in this regard. In fact, autoscaling of serverless functions can provide both reduced latency and efficient resource usage. In this work, we focus on the usage of reinforcement learning to drive resource-based autoscaling of IoT applications on OpenFaaS, the most-adopted open-source serverless platform, running on Kubernetes clusters. We use the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm to dynamically configure the value of the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, trained on a function trace representative of edge IoT traffic taken from the well-known Azure dataset. We discuss the performance of PPO as a function of service parameters in Kubernetes, obtaining an optimal configuration. With this configuration, we compare with state of the art baselines. Then, we delve into state definition, discussing performance and robustness of PPO with respect to traffic burstiness, as well as comparing its performance with an heuristic, which can be considered representative of the long term behavior of a trained Q-Learning approach. We show that, by limiting the features used in state space definition, it is possible to obtain a simpler yet more robust version of PPO, able to perform well under different burstiness of the input process. The price to pay is a small penalty in terms of resource utilization with base PPO when the burstiness of the input process during the test phase matches the one used for the training phase. In addition, we show that the performance of base PPO can be achieved with the designed heuristic, thus without the need of expensive training, provided that tail latency is not a primary requirement. • Study of the impact of state space variables and action space size in performance of PPO for controlling serverless edge computing autoscaling. • Evaluation of sensitivity of trained models to variations in traffic profile burstiness. • Comparison between performance of PPO variants, an a-priori heuristic, and multiple baselines (static HPA, SAC, predictive non reinforcement learning).

Natural language-driven trust requirement elicitation in intent-based networks
abstract: The telecommunication industry has evolved dramatically in recent years and so has its complexity. Due to that, the research and industry community has put the spotlight on developing innovative tools that automate every aspect related to the network management lifecycle, also known as zero-touch network and service management. One of the activities of the utmost importance associated with automated network management is the selection of network and service providers that are going to form an end-to-end connection, even considering multiple domains. In this vein, a pivotal requirement in the context of 6G heterogeneous networks is the representation of trustworthiness and how trust is associated with each network element and its provider. This article addresses such a challenge with the incorporation of Natural Language Processing to build a trust-oriented interpreter which is ultimately leveraged by intent-based network orchestrators. Specifically, this interpreter is designed to process trust requirements in 6G Cloud Continuum scenarios together with an ad-hoc ontology joining three areas such as intent-based networks, trust management, and Cloud Continuum. The interpreter also minimizes the number of interactions between end-users and our system via a context-aware chatbot. Finally, the experiments showcase a high performance of the proposed language model on a synthetic, hand-annotated dataset comprising hundreds of intent and entity samples, indicating an F1-score above 90% for entity recognition, and above 95% in the case of intent recognition when processing trust requirements on intent-based solutions.

Privacy-preserving collaborative threat detection via efficient set intersection cardinality testing
abstract: Collaborative threat detection enables organizations to identify coordinated attacks by correlating their local observations–such as suspicious IP addresses, malware signatures, or flow patterns–with intelligence held by partner entities. However, sharing raw threat data raises confidentiality concerns: organizations may expose sensitive network topology, reveal ongoing investigations, or violate data-protection regulations. A practical middle ground is threshold-based correlation: learning only whether the overlap between two datasets exceeds a significance threshold, without disclosing the actual intersection or its exact size. We formalize this requirement as over-threshold private set intersection cardinality (otPSI-CA) and address the asymmetric setting in which a threat analyst holds a reference indicator set while a partner organization manages multiple datasets (e.g., traffic logs segmented by region or time window). Existing solutions either leak more information than necessary or scale poorly with the number of partner datasets. We propose otPSI-CA ⋆ , a two-round protocol that returns binary decisions–above or below threshold–for all partner datasets simultaneously. Our construction combines a per-bin Fermat’s-little-theorem polynomial encoding with 2048-bit Paillier encryption and a public-constant false-positive correction at the threshold, achieving per-sender end-to-end online response of 0.74 s at n = 100 and 6.57 s at n = 1000 , linear scaling in the number of datasets, and 100% measured decision correctness at the tested ± 10 threshold gap; the realization provides threshold decisions under a quantified false-positive correction, rather than exact threshold testing in all parameter regimes. Compared to a faithfully implemented 2048-bit instantiation of the Ghosh-Simkin (CRYPTO 2019) baseline, the protocol delivers per-sender speedups of three to four orders of magnitude ( 1 0 3 at n = 100 to 4 × 1 0 4 at n = 1000 ); these figures pair our 24-thread implementation against the single-threaded baseline, and the thread-normalized algorithmic speedup is 88 × – 3,770 × , making privacy-preserving threat correlation practical, within the tested parameter regime, for semi-trusted institutional deployments.

CLIN-FL: Cost-efficient Load-balancing for In-Network Federated Learning with non-IID data
abstract: Federated Learning is a popular paradigm for training machine learning models across many devices without sharing their private data, which makes it attractive for deployment in telecommunication and in-network computing environments. However, real-world network data are often heterogeneous, and such feature distribution discrepancies across clients can severely degrade the performance of the global model. While previous works have made notable progress by customizing the aggregation function and designing algorithmic training solutions, limited attention has been directed toward data-centric load balancing techniques that cope with data feature distributions. In this paper, we propose a data load-balancing solution, named CLIN-FL, reducing feature distribution discrepancy in in-network FL by controlling connectivity and latency. We evaluate our approach using both a standard Autoencoder and a Deep Support Vector Data Descriptor (Deep SVDD) based model. Our results show that the proposed CLIN-FL schemes significantly improve feature distribution alignment while enabling a tunable trade-off between anomaly detection accuracy and communication cost, with improvements of up to 38.7% in AUC-ROC (Area Under the ROC Curve) and reductions of up to 20% in communication cost.

DeNoise: A lightweight and tunable defense against AWGN full-band jamming
abstract: Wireless communication systems are increasingly vulnerable to jamming attacks due to the open nature of the medium. Traditional anti-jamming techniques such as Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS) and Direct Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS) are resource-intensive and fail when a jammer disrupts the entire frequency band. This paper presents DeNoise , a lightweight, protocol-agnostic anti-jamming approach that leverages message repetition and ensemble averaging to mitigate any zero-mean random interference, with Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) being the most common and most practically relevant instance. Unlike conventional methods, DeNoise enables successful message decoding even under full-spectrum jamming, at the cost of a reduced bit rate. We evaluate DeNoise through extensive real-world Software-Defined Radio experiments spanning over 720 million I/Q samples across 96 hardware configurations - six jammer waveforms (AWGN, Uniform, Laplacian, Impulse, Narrowband, single-Tone), four spatial scenarios, two jamming powers, and BPSK/QPSK modulations - and complement these with a hybrid Rayleigh/Jakes fading sweep over f d ∈ { 0,5,20,50,200,500,1000 } Hz. In the worst-case spatial configuration (5 m jammer-Rx, 10 m Tx-Rx) under jamming at ＋20 dB above the legitimate signal, BPSK BER drops from 31.6% at a single transmission to 2.1% with 20 repetitions, and QPSK from 38.0% to 4.98%, with consistent improvements across all six jammer waveforms. DeNoise thus offers a robust, tunable solution for restoring communication reliability under aggressive zero-mean jamming.

Conformal prediction for byte-level CPS traffic classification under adversarial attacks
abstract: AI-driven traffic classification is increasingly used in networked cyber–physical systems (CPS) (e.g., smart grids) to enable monitoring from packet-byte representations, without relying on protocol-specific parsing. However, recent work shows that learning-based traffic classifiers can be vulnerable to adaptive adversarial manipulation of observed packet bytes, leading to severe degradation and brittle decisioning at runtime. In this paper, we propose a security-oriented traffic classification framework that integrates adversarial robustness with calibrated uncertainty quantification for CPS networks. Our approach employs a byte-level representation that requires no protocol-specific feature engineering, evaluates robustness under adaptive Carlini–Wagner attacks, and incorporates conformal prediction to provide statistical risk control on predictions during inference. Across multiple CPS traffic datasets, we show that adversarial perturbations substantially reduce classification performance, while adversarial retraining improves robustness. Further, conformal prediction exposes low-confidence regimes and supports reliable operational handling of suspicious or adversarial traffic via selective prediction (accept/reject) with coverage guarantees.

LLM-assisted generation of intentionally vulnerable containerized environments for cyber ranges
abstract: Cyber ranges are essential training platforms for security teams; however, creating intentionally vulnerable environments remains labor-intensive. While modern virtualization technologies like Docker enable “Infrastructure as Code” approaches, and large language models (LLMs) significantly reduce the effort required for code generation, creating exploitable scenarios remains a challenge. It requires resolving dependencies, configuring interconnected services, and ensuring explicit exploit preconditions, yet the effectiveness of LLMs in realizing these scenarios remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a systematic exploratory study of LLM-assisted generation of intentionally vulnerable containerized environments. We compare different generation paradigms (service-based vs. web applications, package-based vs. source-based builds, and single-container vs. compose-based setups) under zero-shot conditions. We evaluate six LLMs using a two-phase protocol: first, we select the model with the lowest mean Weighted Error Score (WES); second, we conduct an in-depth analysis of paired deployment strategies across 22 vulnerabilities (12 services and 10 web applications), totaling 44 generation attempts and 40 analyzed scenarios (following four ethical refusals). Key findings establish a clear feasibility boundary. While state-of-the-art models (e.g., Gemini3-Pro, GPT-5.2) reduced build failure rates from 81.5% to 51.9%, their ability to generate fully functional, exploitable environments remains limited. Specifically, while functional correctness (build/run) reaches 37.5%–50.0% depending on the strategy, the transition to exploitability represents the primary failure point, with only 5.0% (2/40) of analyzed scenarios proving exploitable. We introduce a repair-oriented analysis based on two metrics to evaluate the change impact and automation challenges of fixing incorrect Dockerfiles. This analysis demonstrates that the choice of strategy significantly affects the repair burden: package-based services require higher structural and automation effort than source-based counterparts, while compose-based web deployments yield better functional outcomes than bundled configurations. Furthermore, our results highlight a practical trade-off in service deployment: despite higher build complexity, source-based reconstruction is preferable for vulnerability fidelity. This is because distribution packages often include downstream security backports that silently mitigate vulnerabilities, even when version identifiers suggest susceptibility. Finally, we provide a taxonomy of build, execution, and exploitation errors. All experimental data, including AI-generated Dockerfiles with annotations and prompts, are publicly available. This study establishes both the potential and the current limitations of zero-shot LLM-based generation, serving as a benchmark for future research into tool-augmented approaches.

abstract: Digital Product Passports (DPPs) are emerging as key enablers of Digital Circular Economy (DCE) practices, with upcoming regulations further formalizing their integration, and batteries being the first official use case. Yet, their practical value is related not only to the availability of data through Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, but also to their representative status as the product ages. This work presents BALS-D3QN, a balanced and adaptive scheduler based on the D3QN algorithm, designed to decide when the battery data of a DPP should be updated and resubmitted to an external DLT network, through the Age of Incorrect Information (AoII) metric. Also, BALS-D3QN acts as the decision mechanism of our previous ABS-TD3 solution, by reutilizing the latest observed submission latency of the Shimmer DLT to enable latency-exploratory updates. The proposed framework is evaluated using simulated battery trajectories from products listed within the EPREL database of the European Commission (EC), and compared against key baselines, namely consecutive updates, random policies, and periodic decisions, reflecting different types of behaviors. The results suggest that BALS-D3QN successfully minimizes the congestion impact occurring from the aggressive policies, minimizes the AoII compared to sparse periodic decisions, and showcases better adaptive behavior compared to periodic cases of similar ranges.

Enhancing physical-layer security in THz-based STAR-IRS-assisted symbiotic radio networks using a MADDPG framework
abstract: The integration of terahertz (THz) communications with simultaneously transmitting and reflecting intelligent reflecting surfaces (STAR-IRSs) offers a promising paradigm for sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks, enabling ultra-high data rates and improved physical-layer security. However, dynamic blockage, severe path loss, and multi-zone eavesdropping threats present severe challenges to the secrecy rate maximization in multi-user symbiotic radio (SR) environments. This paper addresses the problem of joint active and passive beamforming optimization to maximize the system secrecy rate under concurrent security threats to primary and secondary users. To solve this non-convex, high-dimensional problem in time-varying THz channels, we develop a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) framework. The framework leverages decentralized, cooperative agents to bypass the high computational complexity of conventional optimization while handling the coupled constraints of STAR-IRS reflection and transmission coefficients. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed MADDPG framework consistently outperforms the single-agent DDPG and successive convex approximation (SCA) baselines across different numbers of base station (BS) antennas, STAR-IRS elements, and transmit-power levels. At normal conditions, MADDPG achieves a secrecy rate of 5.25 bps/Hz, corresponding to improvements of 22% and 31% over DDPG and SCA, respectively.

title: uBPF-based network intrusion detection and prevention systems empowered by machine learning algorithms
abstract: Network Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (NIDPSs) play a crucial role in identifying and blocking malicious traffic. In-kernel NIDPSs leveraging extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) have achieved high detection performance and throughput by operating directly in kernel space. However, eBPF-based NIDPSs face portability challenges across diverse runtime environments, limiting their deployment on kernel-bypassing frameworks such as AF_XDP and the Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK). In this paper, we propose a userspace BPF (uBPF)-based NIDPS empowered by machine learning (ML) algorithms and integrate it with kernel-bypassing frameworks to achieve portability across diverse runtime environments while accurately and efficiently detecting and preventing Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. We evaluate the proposed NIDPSs from both DDoS detection performance and packet processing performance perspectives. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed NIDPS achieves high classification performance for DDoS detection, while enabling the same uBPF-based detection logic to operate across different packet processing frameworks. Moreover, the uBPF-based NIDPSs running on the DPDK data plane achieve packet processing rates 3.38–8.60 × higher than the evaluated in-kernel NIDPS implementations.

Building a supervised–unsupervised ensemble for intrusion detection systems using model calibration and decision fusion
abstract: Machine learning, particularly deep learning, has become a prominent approach to network intrusion detection because it can learn patterns from network traffic and adapt to evolving threats. However, most existing Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) approaches address only one side of the problem: they either classify known attacks from labeled data or detect previously unseen attacks through anomaly detection. In operational network environments, both capabilities are required within a single adaptive system. To address this limitation, we propose a hybrid IDS that combines supervised and unsupervised models in a calibration-aware ensemble designed to detect both known attacks and attack classes absent from the training data. The main contribution of this work is a calibration and decision fusion pipeline that aligns the outputs of heterogeneous models and integrates them into a unified detection decision. Experiments conducted using two benchmark datasets, CIC-IDS2017 and BoT-IoT, across different experimental settings, show that the proposed ensemble is capable of both detecting previously unseen attacks and performing multiclass classification of known attacks, while maintaining comparable multiclass performance despite the increased task complexity. It also improves binary detection performance, indicating that the hybrid design successfully exploits the complementary strengths of supervised classification and unsupervised anomaly detection.
